Beatle Mania Hits Sour Note

IFrom Tribune Wire Services)
Brian Epstein, Beatle’s man-
ager, cut short his vacation in
Europe and flew to New York
last night to quell the furor
aroused in the United States by
Beatle John Lennon’s state-
ment that the singing group
was “more popular than
Jesus.” Epstein said Lennon
had been misinterpreted.
Epstein told newsmen at Ken-
nedy International airport that
the current uproar was “‘the
normal sort of Beatle furor.”
Epstein was asked if he
thought the Beatles had lost
face because of the remark.
“T don’t know,” Epstein said.
“This-is why I’ve come. I want
to avoid any further misinter-
pretation.”
Plan Tour of U. S.
The Beatles are scheduled to
begin a 14-city, four-week tour
of the United States next Thurs-
day. Epstein was asked if there
was a chance the tour might be |
canceled.
“No,” he said, “not at this
stage.” |
Epstein did ‘not deny that
Lennon made the remark at-
tributed to him, But. when a
newsman asked Epstein if he:
actually believed the Beatles
were more popular than Jesus,
he snapped, “Of course not.”
Keith. Howell, a spokesman
for the singing group in Lon-
don, had said earlier that Ep-
stein cut short a vacation ‘to
fly to the United States and
“assess the situation.”
Will Issue Statement
_ Epstein said he planned. to
‘meet today with officials of the
General Artists corporation, the
firm that represents the Beatles
'in the United States, and issue
a statement later.
“To avoid further confusion
and misinterpretation, neither
John nor the other Beatles are
commenting immediately,”
Howell had said in London.
An estimated 35 radio stations
in 15 states and one in Mani-
'toba, Canada, announced they
| would no longer play Beatles’
records because of the remarks
by Lennon.
The Beatie boycott. was begun
last week in Birmingham, Ala.,
by two disk jockeys who took
| offense at the statements attrib-
‘uted to Lennon in the article.
“The remarks are quoted out
of a series of articles done by
Maureen Cleave of the [London]
Evening Standard last Febru-
ary and March,” Howell said.
The series was printed in an
American magazine, Datebook.
“Christianity will. go,” Len-

John Lennon

non was quoted as saying. “It
will go . . . it will vanish and
shrink. I needn’t argue about
that, I’m right and I will be
proved right.
“We are more popular than
Jesus now: I don’t know which
will go first—rock ‘n’ roll or
Christianity. Jesus was all

| right, but -his. disciples were

thick and ordinary.”
Tommy Charles, station man-
ager of WAQY in Birmingham,
who sparked the drive along
wiht Doug Layton, said the
Beatles were banned because
“we just felt it was so. absurd
and sacrilegicus that something
ought to be done to show them
they cannot get away with this
sort of thing.”

Stations Plan Bonfires

Several radio stations sched-
uled- bonfires for the burning
of Beatle records and pictures.
Other. stations. said they
would wait until they checked
the authenticity of the quote;
others polled listeners and most
reported that the polls over-
whelmingly supported a ban of
the Beatles.
Donald Ballou, 35, general
manager of WSLB, Ogdensburg,
N. Y., declared that the Beatles
are “off my station.”
“Until John Lennon retracts

his anti-Christ statement, KTEE
will play no more Beatles’ rec-
ords,” said Johnny Midnight at
KTEE, Idaho Falls, Idaho.
In Milwaukee, King Zhornik,
music director of WRIT, said
the Beatles would not be banned
until he saw Lennon’s remarks
in print. But “I can’t believe
he said it,’ Zbornik declared.
“I’ve been fed up with them
ever since their latest album
came out with a terrible cover
on it. The way these guys have
been acting lately is a real let-
down for our kids. If they’re
going to take all of the Amer-
ican kids’ money, at least they
could be gentlemen about it.”
Supports Beatle Remark
“T think John Lennon is
right,” said Norm Seeley, mu-
sic director of KRUX in
Phoenix Ariz. “We have placed
more emphasis on material and
physical things than religion.
Religion in itself is good and
wholesome but it’s our fault
that it’s on its way out.”
